report:
Conclusion: the claim is not supported. Apples naturally make cuticular wax; washing can remove some, so packers may add a thin edible coating to limit moisture loss and bruising (http://nwhort.org/fruitcoatings/). The relevant question is whether approved coating ingredients are carcinogenic at food-use exposures.

For carnauba wax, FDA lists it among “Substances Added to Food,” reflecting permitted food use rather than a cancer hazard finding (https://hfpappexternal.fda.gov/scripts/fdcc/index.cfm?set=FoodSubstances&id=CARNAUBAWAX). EFSA’s re-evaluation of carnauba wax (E 903) notes it is authorized as a glazing agent and treats it as poorly absorbed; it did not establish an ADI mainly because long-term data were limited, but it did not conclude that normal food uses cause cancer (https://www.efsa.europa.eu/el/efsajournal/pub/2880). For shellac (E 904), EFSA’s 2024 re-evaluation set a temporary ADI only for wax-free chemically bleached shellac while impurity data are generated, and explicitly said that ADI is not applicable to wax-containing shellac; again, this is a data-gap/impurity issue, not evidence that apple coatings cause cancer (https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2024.8897).

The “wax causes cancer” view appears to rest on confusion with non-food petroleum products, pesticide-residue anxiety, and social-media demonstrations. Evidence supports normal washing; peeling is optional, not necessary for cancer avoidance.
